newsitem.title: HUNGARY: FOCUS-Budapest bucks trend on E.European bourses.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Budapest bucks trend on E.European bourses.

text.p: A strong dollar and investors taking refuge in Hungarian shares helped the Budapest bourse to reverse the bearish tone plaguing most East European markets this week.
Floods depressed Polish and Czech stocks, while Bratislava and Bucharest bourses also fell. Blue-chip gains pushed Zagreb and Ljubliana shares higher.
Apart from the Budapest bourse, exchanges in the region were unmoved by this week's strong gains on Wall Street.
The Central European Share Index (CESI), which follows price movements in 72 Hungarian, Polish, Czech, Slovak and Slovenian shares, fell 0.21 percent on the week to close at 1,414.7 points on Friday.
BUDAPEST

The Budapest Stock Exchange coasted to three consecutive record highs this week, mainly on the back of a strong dollar, which made the forint, and therefore Hungarian shares, cheaper for foreigners. The mid-week Dow Jones rally also boosted the trend.
"Conditions are steady, the dollar is 1.83 (to the mark), the Dow Jones firmed again and there are still floods (in the Czech Republic and Poland)," one trader said.
Market participants said money had left the Polish and Czech markets in search of safer investment opportunities in Hungary, even though some analysts think many Hungarian shares are overvalued.
WARSAW
Polish shares fell 1.9 percent to 15,056.8 points this week and analysts said the market should maintain its slight downtrend on macroeconomic concerns into next week.

"Generally the market is slipping the whole time, you can't see demand from foreign investors and you can see there are expectations of an interest-rate rise, especially as money supply is rising," said Czeslaw Pospieszynski of PBI brokerage.

Analysts said floods, which swamped more than one percent of the country, had gripped the market as they could lead to the central bank lending up to 2.5 billion zlotys ($723 million) to the government.
Forex leaders have said immediate official rate rise expectations subsided but that the central bank might increase market rates quickly to cool growing domestic demand.
They also said the run-up to parliamentary elections due on September 21 should help continue a slight bearish trend.
PRAGUE

Czech shares traded slightly lower throughout the week, led by the most heavily capitalised banking issue, Komercni Banka, which dealers said had been hit by concerns that flooding in the Czech Republic could eat into profits.
Around one third of the country has been affected by the floods and Komercni, whose portfolio is dominated by commercial loans, is thought to be more exposed than other banks.
Komercni was down 24 crowns, or 1.5 percent, over the week, closing at 1,616 on Friday. The PX50 index fell 0.2 percent on the week.
BRATISLAVA
The Bratislava Stock Exchange (BSE) extended a long-term sluggish mood this week, with the official 16-share SAX index dropping by 2.04 points, or 1.20 percent.
The SAX fell to a year-low of 164.81 points on Tuesday, but rebounded with slight gains to close at 167.27 on Friday.
Brokers said several factors had prompted the lacklustre mood over the past few weeks, including little interest among foreign investors.
They said improvements in trading activity could only be expected when liquidity shortages in the local money market ended as investors were being lured by higher interest rates.
BUCHAREST
Profit-taking was the main feature on the Bucharest stock exchange during the week, putting pressure on high-caps and pushing three unofficial indexes lower on Friday.
Traders said some bargain hunters emerged on the second-tier but low liquidity had capped strong gains, keeping the overall market in a bearish mood.
LJUBLJANA
Slovenian shares jumped 6.13 percent this week, with the blue-chip SBI index surging 90.58 points to 1,568.79.

Market participants said the index was likely to continue rising over the summer as domestic investors are expected to follow international buyers' activity. The blue-chip index is forecast to rise by 30 to 50 percent over the summer.
ZAGREB
Croatian top shares, drugs concern Pliva and Zagrebacka Banka traded heavily this week, both hitting their all-time highs on the back of the strong dollar.
Recently-floated ship repairer Viktor Lenac was also active, as was blue chip Varazdinska Banka.
Traders predicted a short-term bullish trend next week.
